title.value: Where Telehealth Revenue Leaks, and How We Stop It

paragraph.value: Telehealth is a routine part of care now. FAIR Health found that 18.4% of commercially insured patients had a telehealth claim in the first quarter of 2026, and more than half of them (52.1%) were seen for a mental health condition. With that much volume, a single medicine billing habit repeated across every virtual visit turns into a steady loss. These are the leaks we look for first.

The patient was at home, but the claim says POS 02. Medicare pays the visit at the lower facility rate and nothing gets denied, so the shortfall can go unnoticed for months. We set POS from the patient location recorded in the note, then check every payment against the rate it should have paid.

title.value: Modifiers That Don’t Match the Visit

paragraph.value: A phone visit goes out with modifier 95, or a commercial video visit goes out without the 95 the plan requires. Either one can be denied now or recouped after an audit. We build each payer’s modifier rules into our claim edits, so a mismatch is caught before the claim is submitted.

title.value: The Wrong Code Set for the Payer

paragraph.value: Medicare won’t pay the AMA’s 98000-series telemedicine codes. Some commercial plans have the opposite rule and deny office E/M codes for virtual visits. Our experts code every claim on its payer’s track, so each one goes out with the codes that payer actually pays.

Not every service can be billed as telehealth. Medicare limits it to its Telehealth Services List, commercial plans write their own policies and audio-only has tighter limits still. We check telehealth and audio-only coverage before the visit, while there’s still time to schedule it differently.

title.value: Virtual Check-Ins Billed Inside Excluded Timeframes

paragraph.value: Virtual check-ins and e-visits come with timing rules, and auditors are checking them. In April 2026, the OIG reported about $2.26 million in potentially improper Medicare payments for these services, most of it for check-ins billed inside the period the code excludes.

title.value: Clinicians Not Licensed in the Patient’s State

paragraph.value: If the clinician isn’t licensed where the patient is, or isn’t enrolled with that state’s payer, the claim can’t be paid. Clean coding won’t fix it. MedCare MSO tracks licensure and enrollment by clinician and state, so a gap shows up before the visit instead of after the denial.

A telehealth note has to show the modality, where the patient was, the patient’s consent, and for time-based codes, the time. When something is missing, the payment stays open to recoupment after an audit. Our team flags incomplete notes before coding, while your clinician can still add what’s missing.

title.value: Telehealth Billing Under Two Rulebooks: Medicare vs Commercial and Medicaid

paragraph.value: Medicare bills a virtual visit with the same E/M codes used in the office and flags it as telehealth through place of service and modifiers. Many commercial plans use the AMA’s telemedicine codes instead, and Medicaid sets its own rules in every state. That’s why telehealth billing only gets reliable when your team treats these as separate rulebooks. We code each claim on the track that matches the payer receiving it.

paragraph.value: Medicare Advantage plans must cover at least what traditional Medicare covers, and many add telehealth benefits of their own, so we check each plan’s policy. Where a state’s parity law requires the in-person rate, we hold commercial payments to it.
POS 02 vs POS 10: Which One Applies?

Use POS 10 when the patient is at home during the visit and POS 02 when they’re anywhere else, like a clinic or their workplace. It sounds like a small choice, but it changes the payment. Since January 1, 2024, Medicare has paid telehealth to patients at home at the non-facility rate, while POS 02 claims get the lower facility rate. Commercial plans set their own POS rules, so check each one.

paragraph.value: What do MedCare MSO’s telehealth billing services include?

Everything from the benefit check before the visit to the final payment. We code each telehealth claim with the right place of service and modifiers, scrub it against the payer’s telehealth policy, submit it, post the payment and check that it paid in full. Denials and A/R follow-up are included too, and so are credentialing and payer enrollment in every state your clinicians serve.
How much does MedCare MSO charge for telehealth billing?

Most practices pay 3–7% of net collections, depending on specialty, volume and the services you need. There are no setup fees or hidden costs, and terms are month-to-month, so you’re never locked into a long contract. We only earn when you get paid, which ties our results to yours. Your free billing analysis comes with a quote based on your own numbers.
Can MedCare MSO work with our EHR and telehealth platform?

Yes. We connect to your EHR and practice management system during onboarding, and we also offer our own platforms, HealUS EHR and Maximus PMS, if you need them. Your clinicians keep using the billing for telehealth platform they already have, so nothing changes for them.
Can you bill telehealth for clinicians who see patients in several states?

Yes. Licensure generally follows where the patient is during the visit, and each state needs its own payer enrollment, including a separate Medicare enrollment. Interstate compacts like the IMLC, PSYPACT and the Nurse Licensure Compact can make multi-state licensing faster. Our credentialing team keeps enrollment and revalidation current for each clinician in each state, so claims don’t stall over paperwork.
Do you sign a Business Associate Agreement?

Yes. HIPAA requires a BAA with any vendor that handles your patients’ protected health information, and we sign ours before we see any patient data. Your free billing analysis doesn’t use patient data, so the BAA is signed when we start working on your actual claims. Our operations are HIPAA-compliant, with HITRUST and SOC 2 certification.
Which modifier is used for telehealth: 95, 93 or GT?

Modifier 95 marks a real-time audio-video visit, and modifier 93 marks an audio-only one. GT is now limited to a few specific billing situations. Codes that already describe how the visit happened, like the 98000-series, usually don’t need a modifier at all. Each payer has the final say, which is why our claim edits apply modifier rules payer by payer.
Does Medicare pay for CPT codes 98000–98015?

No. Medicare doesn’t pay the AMA’s telemedicine E/M codes 98000–98015. It pays telehealth E/M visits under 99202–99215 instead, with a telehealth place of service and modifier. The one exception in the series is CPT 98016, the brief virtual check-in. Many commercial plans do accept the 98000-series, so we code each claim for the payer that’s receiving it.
Can G2211 be billed with a telehealth visit?

Yes. Medicare allows the G2211 complexity add-on on office and outpatient E/M visits delivered by telehealth, as long as the documentation shows an ongoing care relationship. It usually can’t be billed when the E/M carries modifier 25, unless the 25 is for a preventive service. CMS is replacing G2211 with modifier B1 in 2027, and our coders apply whichever rule covers the date of service.
Is telehealth billing the same as telemedicine billing?

In practice, yes. Payers and billing teams use the two terms interchangeably. Strictly speaking, telehealth is the broader one, since it also covers remote monitoring and e-visits, not just live visits. Medicare even treats virtual check-ins and e-visits as communication technology-based services, separate from its Telehealth Services List. We bill each service under the rules that apply to it.
